title: Game_theory
summary:
Game theory is the study of mathematical models of strategic interactions. It has applications in many fields of social science, and is used extensively in economics, logic, systems science and computer science. It is now an umbrella term for the science of rational decision making in humans, animals, and computers.

Initially, game theory addressed two-person zero-sum games, in which a participants gains or losses are exactly balanced by the losses and gains of the other participant. In the 1950s, it was extended to the study of non zero-sum games, and was eventually applied to a wide range of behavioral relations. Modern game theory began with the idea of mixed-strategy equilibria in two-person zero-sum games and its proof by John von Neumann. His paper was followed by Theory of Games and Economic Behavior (1944), co-written with Oskar Morgenstern, which considered cooperative games of several players.

Game theory experienced a flurry of activity in the 1950s, during which the concepts of the core, the extensive form game, fictitious play, repeated games, and the Shapley value were developed. The first mathematical discussion of the prisoners dilemma appeared, and an experiment was undertaken by mathematicians Merrill M. Flood and Melvin Dresher, as part of the RAND Corporations investigations into game theory. In 1965, Reinhard Selten introduced his solution concept of subgame perfect equilibria. In 1994, Nash, Selten and Harsanyi became Economics Nobel Laureates for their contributions to economic game theory.

Applications extend to biology, where payoffs are often interpreted as corresponding to fitness, and to cybersecurity, where tools automate the transformation of vulnerability data into models allowing defenders to synthesize optimal defence strategies. Fifteen game theorists have won the Nobel Prize in economics as of 2020.
